terms.def: highest price a buyer will pay / lowest a seller will accept; the gap is the spread.
bid–ask difference; a direct trading cost, wider in thin names and after hours.
executes immediately at the best available price; guarantees fill, not price.
executes only at a stated price or better; guarantees price, not fill.
becomes a market order once a trigger price trades; used to exit losers.
becomes a limit order at trigger; can fail to fill in a fast move.
stop that moves with price by a fixed amount or percent, locking in gains.
how long an order lives: day, good-till-canceled (GTC), immediate-or-cancel (IOC), fill-or-kill (FOK).
pre-market and after-hours sessions; thinner liquidity, wider spreads, limit orders only on most platforms.
ease of trading size without moving price; measured by volume and depth.
visible resting bids and asks at each price level.
difference between expected and actual fill price.
order executed for fewer shares than requested.
round lot is 100 shares; odd lots are anything smaller.
trade date plus one business day before cash and shares officially change hands.
shares traded in a period; confirms or contradicts price moves.
price opens away from the prior close; gap up / gap down.
exchange pause in trading, usually for news or volatility.
open, high, low, close; the four prices that make a candle or bar.
chart bar showing OHLC with a body and wicks; color indicates direction.
price level where buying has repeatedly stopped declines.
price level where selling has repeatedly stopped advances.
sequence of higher highs and higher lows (uptrend) or the reverse.
arithmetic mean of the last N closes.
weighted mean that reacts faster to recent prices.
50-day SMA crossing above / below the 200-day.
0–100 momentum oscillator; conventionally under 30 oversold, over 70 overbought.
difference between 12- and 26-period EMAs plus a 9-period signal line; crossovers flag momentum shifts.
SMA with bands at ±2 standard deviations; width tracks volatility.
average of recent bar ranges; a volatility measure used to size stops.
volume-weighted average price for the session; institutional benchmark.
position of the close within the recent high–low range.
price makes a new high or low that the indicator does not confirm.
price moves through support or resistance on rising volume.
assumption that stretched prices return toward an average.
assumption that recent direction persists.
indicator readings suggesting a move is stretched; not a signal by itself.
number of bars an indicator uses; the main tuning knob.
share price × shares outstanding.
net income ÷ shares outstanding.
price ÷ EPS; trailing uses the last four quarters, forward uses estimates.
P/E ÷ expected earnings growth rate.
top-line sales before any costs.
profit at each stage as a percent of revenue.
operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.
total liabilities ÷ shareholder equity; leverage measure.
annual dividend ÷ share price.
first day a buyer no longer receives the declared dividend.
quarterly results release; the highest-volatility scheduled event for a stock.
management's forward projections; misses drive most post-earnings moves.
annual report, quarterly report, material-event filing.
officer or director buys and sells, filed within two business days.
average of published estimates and price targets.
dollars or shares committed to one trade.
amount you accept losing if the stop is hit; commonly 0.5–2% of account.
entry price minus stop price; combined with risk per trade, it determines size.
potential gain ÷ potential loss at the planned exit points.
(win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss); the only number that says whether a rule makes money.
percent of trades closed at a profit; meaningless without average win and loss.
peak-to-trough decline in account value.
the largest drawdown over a period; the pain metric.
a completed buy-and-sell (or sell-and-cover) pair.
closed profit or loss vs. open mark-to-market.
entering or exiting in tranches instead of all at once.
degree to which positions move together; concentrated correlation is hidden size.
spreading exposure across uncorrelated positions.
borrowing to increase position size; amplifies both directions.
broker demand for cash when equity falls below the maintenance requirement.
four or more day trades in five business days in a margin account triggers a $25,000 equity minimum.
cash plus available margin.
formula for the bet size that maximizes long-run growth; usually applied at a fraction.
record of thesis, entry, exit, size, and outcome; the raw material for every review.
structured review of a closed trade against its original thesis.
purchase price plus commissions; the starting point for gain calculations.
a specific purchase batch with its own basis and date.
method for choosing which lot a sale closes; changes the taxable gain.
held one year or less vs. more than one year; taxed at different rates.
selling at a loss and rebuying substantially identical shares within 30 days before or after; the loss is deferred.
net losses beyond the annual deduction limit carry to future years.
broker's annual report of sales and basis.
dividend taxed at long-term rates if holding-period rules are met.
valuing open positions at current price; also an election available to trader-status filers.
IRS classification for high-frequency, full-time traders; hard to qualify for.
federal regulator of securities markets and issuers.
self-regulatory body for broker-dealers and registered representatives.
firm that executes trades for customers or its own account; registered with SEC and FINRA.
firm or person paid to give individualized investment advice; registered with SEC or a state.
obligation to act in the client's best interest; applies to RIAs.
Advisers Act carve-out for impersonal, general, regularly circulated publications; the line an education product must stay behind.
recommendations tailored to a specific person's situation; the trigger for RIA registration.
standard broker-dealers owe retail customers when recommending securities.
trading on material non-public information; illegal regardless of how it was obtained.
pump-and-dump, spoofing, wash trading; illegal.
income or net-worth threshold that unlocks private offerings.
older broker standard: recommendation must fit the customer's profile.
insures brokerage accounts against firm failure, not against losses.
required plain-language statements that content is educational and not advice.
LLM plus tools plus a loop that observes, reasons, acts, and repeats.
structured request from the model to an external function (get quote, place order).
open standard for exposing tools to a model; Robinhood and others ship MCP servers.
programmatic interface for quotes, orders, and positions (Robinhood, Alpaca, Interactive Brokers).
simulated account with real prices and fake money; the only environment for learning.
every consequential action waits for explicit human approval.
the specific checkpoint where an order is proposed but not sent.
dry-run API call returning cost, fees, and buying-power impact without executing.
condition the agent evaluates on a schedule (e.g., RSI below a threshold).
condition that fires a rule; price level, indicator value, time, or news.
notification that a trigger fired; the agent's lowest-risk output.
mechanism that runs the agent at fixed intervals.
standing instructions defining the agent's role, limits, and forbidden actions.
model response constrained to a schema (JSON) so code can act on it.
technique forcing the model to emit only valid structured output.
hard-coded check outside the model: max position size, allowed symbols, order-type whitelist.
designing actions so a retry does not place a duplicate order.
immutable record of every observation, reasoning step, proposal, and approval.
model states a price, fill, or position that does not exist; why every fact must come from a tool result.
model rationalizes a trade it already leaned toward; countered by requiring a stated invalidation condition.
running a rule against historical data; useful, and easy to overfit.
rule tuned so tightly to past data that it fails on new data.
single action that halts the agent and cancels open orders.

scenarios.stem: A stock shows bid 41.20 / ask 41.28. You place a market order to buy 100 shares during regular hours. What is your most likely fill?
scenarios.rationale: Market buys take the ask; market sells take the bid. The 8-cent spread is your cost.

scenarios.stem: You place a limit buy at 41.00 while the ask is 41.28. Price drifts to 41.05 and then rallies to 44. What happened to your order?
scenarios.rationale: A limit order only fills at its price or better. Price never reached 41.00.

scenarios.stem: You own shares bought at 50 and place a stop order at 46. Overnight, bad news gaps the stock open at 40. Where does your stop fill?
scenarios.rationale: A stop becomes a market order once 46 trades; the first trade is near 40, so that's where it executes.

scenarios.stem: Same setup as A3, but you used a stop-limit with stop 46 and limit 45.50. What happens on the gap to 40?
options: Does not fill; you still hold
scenarios.rationale: The stop triggers a limit at 45.50, but price is below that, so nothing executes. Stop-limits protect price, not exit.

scenarios.stem: You submit a limit order at 3:58 p.m. with time in force "day." It's unfilled at the close. What is its status at 9:30 a.m. the next day?
scenarios.rationale: Day orders expire at session close.

scenarios.stem: A thinly traded stock averages 30,000 shares a day. Your agent proposes a market order for 5,000 shares. What is the main risk?
scenarios.rationale: You are 17% of daily volume; the order will walk up the book. Use limits and scale in.

scenarios.stem: You sold shares on Monday. When can you withdraw the cash?
scenarios.rationale: U.S. equity settlement is T+1.

scenarios.stem: Your agent places a limit order for 500 shares; the fill report shows 300. What should the next step be?
options: Recognize a partial fill and decide whether to keep the remaining 200 working
scenarios.rationale: The remaining 200 are still resting. Duplicating the order overbuys.

scenarios.stem: A trailing stop of 5% is set on a position bought at 100. Price rises to 120, then falls. Where does the stop trigger?
scenarios.rationale: The stop ratchets up to 5% below the peak (120 × 0.95).

scenarios.stem: At 7:15 a.m. your agent flags a pre-market gap and proposes a market buy. Why should the guardrail reject it?
options: Most platforms allow only limit orders in extended hours, and spreads are wide
The stop rule doesn't apply pre-market
scenarios.rationale: Extended-hours liquidity is thin; a market order there is a slippage trap and usually not permitted anyway.

scenarios.stem: A 14-period RSI reads 26. What does this tell you on its own?
options: Momentum has been strongly negative recently
scenarios.rationale: RSI measures recent momentum, not value or direction of the next move.

scenarios.stem: Price has been making higher highs for three weeks while RSI makes lower highs. Name the pattern.
scenarios.rationale: Price and indicator disagree; momentum is weakening under the rally.

scenarios.stem: The 50-day SMA crosses above the 200-day SMA. Which is true?
options: Called a golden cross; a lagging trend signal
scenarios.rationale: Moving-average crosses confirm trends late; they don't predict.

scenarios.stem: MACD line crosses above its signal line while the histogram flips positive. What is this generally read as?
scenarios.rationale: The faster EMA is pulling ahead of the slower one.

scenarios.stem: Bollinger Bands have narrowed to their tightest width in six months. What does that suggest?
options: Low volatility, often preceding an expansion
scenarios.rationale: Band width measures volatility, not direction.

scenarios.stem: ATR is 2.40 on a 60-dollar stock. Your rule sets stops at 2× ATR. Where is the initial stop for a long entry at 60?
Price breaks above a resistance level that held four times, on volume 40% below average. How confident should the rule be?
options: Low; breakouts without volume often fail
High; four tests means strong level
scenarios.rationale: Volume is the confirmation for a breakout.

scenarios.stem: Your agent uses a 5-period RSI instead of 14. What changes?
scenarios.rationale: Shorter lookbacks react faster and whipsaw more.

scenarios.stem: Price is trading well below VWAP all session. What does that describe?
scenarios.rationale: Average trade has printed above current price.

scenarios.stem: A mean-reversion rule and a momentum rule both fire on the same stock, in opposite directions. What is the correct response?
options: Neither; the rules conflict, and the agent should log and skip
scenarios.rationale: Conflicting signals are information; a supervised agent flags them rather than picking one arbitrarily.

scenarios.stem: RSI has stayed above 70 for three weeks during a strong uptrend. What does that show?
options: Strong trends can pin oscillators at extremes
scenarios.rationale: "Overbought" is a description, not a trigger.

scenarios.stem: Your rule says "RSI below 30." The stock's RSI hits 30.4 at the close and 29.8 in after-hours. Should the rule fire?
options: Depends on how the rule defines the bar — the spec must say
scenarios.rationale: Ambiguous rules produce ambiguous agents. Define the session and bar type in the rule.

scenarios.stem: A company has 200 million shares at 45 dollars. Its market cap is:
Trailing EPS is 3.00 and the stock trades at 60. Trailing P/E is:
Two companies both trade at 25× earnings. One grows earnings 5% a year, the other 25%. Which has the lower PEG?
scenarios.rationale: PEG = P/E ÷ growth: 5 vs. 1.

scenarios.stem: Earnings beat estimates but the stock falls 12%. Most likely cause?
scenarios.rationale: The market trades on the future; guidance beats the print.

scenarios.stem: A stock declares a 1-dollar dividend with ex-date Thursday. You buy Thursday morning. Do you receive it?
scenarios.rationale: Buyers on or after the ex-date do not receive the declared dividend.

scenarios.stem: A Form 4 shows the CFO bought 50,000 shares on the open market. What is that?
scenarios.rationale: Insiders may trade with disclosure and outside blackout windows.

scenarios.stem: Operating cash flow is 800M; capex is 300M. Free cash flow is:
scenarios.rationale: OCF − capex.

scenarios.stem: Your agent pulls an EPS figure from its own memory instead of a filing or data API. Why is this a problem?
options: The number may be hallucinated; every fact must come from a tool result
scenarios.rationale: Model recall is not a data source.

scenarios.stem: Account is 20,000. Risk per trade is 1%. Entry 50, stop 47. Position size?
scenarios.rationale: Risk 200 dollars ÷ 3 dollars stop distance = 66.7; round down.

scenarios.stem: Same account, same risk. Entry 50, stop 49.50. Position size?
scenarios.rationale: 200 ÷ 0.50. Tighter stops mean bigger size — and more whipsaw.

scenarios.stem: A rule wins 40% of the time. Average win 300, average loss 100. Expectancy per trade?
A rule wins 80% of the time. Average win 50, average loss 300. Expectancy?
scenarios.rationale: (0.8 × 50) − (0.2 × 300). High win rate, losing rule.

scenarios.stem: Account peaks at 25,000, falls to 20,000, recovers to 23,000. Max drawdown?
You need what percent gain to recover from a 50% drawdown?
scenarios.rationale: Losses compound against you.

scenarios.stem: Your agent holds five positions in five semiconductor stocks, each sized at 1% risk. Effective risk is closer to:
scenarios.rationale: Correlated positions are one big position.

scenarios.stem: A cash account of 8,000 makes four day trades in a week. What happens?
options: Nothing; PDT applies to margin accounts
scenarios.rationale: The PDT rule applies to margin accounts; cash accounts face settled-funds limits instead.

scenarios.stem: A margin account with 20,000 equity makes four day trades in five business days. Result?
options: Flagged as pattern day trader; restricted until equity reaches 25,000
scenarios.rationale: The 25,000 minimum is the PDT threshold.

scenarios.stem: Position is up 15%. Your plan said take half at 10% and trail the rest. What is the correct action?
options: Follow the plan: scale out half, trail the remainder
scenarios.rationale: Plans exist to remove in-the-moment decisions.

scenarios.stem: A trade thesis was "breakout above 80 on volume." Price broke 80 on low volume and reversed. The trade lost. What goes in the post-mortem?
options: The volume condition was not met; entry violated the thesis
scenarios.rationale: The post-mortem checks execution against the thesis, not outcome.

scenarios.stem: A trade followed every rule and lost. What goes in the journal?
options: Good process, bad outcome; no change from one trade
scenarios.rationale: Rules are judged over samples, not single trades.

scenarios.stem: Kelly says bet 20% of the account. Practitioners typically use:
options: A fraction, often a quarter to half
scenarios.rationale: Full Kelly assumes perfect estimates and tolerates severe drawdowns.

scenarios.stem: Your buying power reads 40,000 on 20,000 cash. What is that?
scenarios.rationale: Standard Reg T margin.

scenarios.stem: Equity falls below maintenance and the broker issues a margin call. What are your options?
options: Deposit cash or close positions; the broker may liquidate for you
scenarios.rationale: Margin calls are not optional.

scenarios.stem: You bought 100 shares at 40 and 100 at 60. You sell 100 at 55 using FIFO. Taxable gain?
scenarios.rationale: FIFO closes the 40-dollar lot: (55 − 40) × 100.

scenarios.stem: Same lots, but you select the 60-dollar lot specifically. Result?
scenarios.rationale: Specific-ID lets you choose; (55 − 60) × 100.

scenarios.stem: You sell at a loss on March 1 and buy the same stock on March 20. What happens to the loss?
options: Disallowed now and added to the new lot's basis (wash sale)
scenarios.rationale: 30-day window before and after.

scenarios.stem: Shares bought June 10, 2025 and sold June 10, 2026. Holding period?
options: Exactly one year counts as long-term
scenarios.rationale: Long-term requires more than one year; sell June 11 or later.

scenarios.stem: Net capital losses for the year are 9,000. What happens on the federal return?
options: 3,000 deducted against ordinary income; 6,000 carried forward
scenarios.rationale: Standard annual limit and carryforward.

scenarios.stem: Your agent's journal records fills but not cost basis or lot dates. What does that break?
scenarios.rationale: Basis and dates are the tax record.

scenarios.stem: A dividend on shares held 15 days around the ex-date is:
scenarios.rationale: Qualified status requires a 61-day holding window.

scenarios.stem: A part-time trader with 40 trades a year wants trader tax status. Likelihood?
options: Low; TTS requires substantial, frequent, continuous activity
scenarios.rationale: Few retail traders qualify.

scenarios.stem: Your site publishes a weekly "what our agent flagged" newsletter to all subscribers with the same content. Is this investment advice requiring registration?
options: Generally no; impersonal, general circulation fits the publisher's exclusion
scenarios.rationale: Impersonal and regular is the key.

scenarios.stem: A subscriber emails: "I have 30k and I'm 55 — should I buy CHRW?" You reply "yes, 20% of your account." What did you just do?
scenarios.rationale: Tailoring to a person's situation triggers registration.

scenarios.stem: You offer to run your agent on a subscriber's Robinhood account for 20% of profits. What's the issue?
options: Managing others' accounts for compensation requires RIA registration; performance fees have their own limits
scenarios.rationale: Discretionary management is the clearest RIA trigger.

scenarios.stem: Your landing page says "Our agent returned 34% last quarter." What should compliance flag?
options: Performance claim: needs substantiation, disclosures, and invites scrutiny; better to show process
scenarios.rationale: Advertising rules and plain risk.

scenarios.stem: A subscriber posts screenshots of paper-trade results and calls them real. Your responsibility?
options: Correct the record; your platform labels paper results clearly
scenarios.rationale: Mislabeled simulated results are a misrepresentation risk for you.

scenarios.stem: A friend at a company tells you earnings will miss; you sell before the announcement. This is:
options: Legal in a paper account only
scenarios.rationale: Material non-public information, regardless of source.

scenarios.stem: Placing and canceling large orders to move price without intending to fill is:
Which body registers and examines broker-dealers?
A brokerage fails. SIPC covers:
options: Missing securities and cash up to limits

scenarios.stem: Your app lets users write rules and run them on their own paper account. No recommendations are made. Which is the safest description of the product?
scenarios.rationale: Keep the language matching the function.

scenarios.stem: A credit-union prospect asks whether the Agent OS trading module can execute on member accounts. Correct answer?
options: It can supervise and log; execution on customer accounts is a regulated activity the institution must own
scenarios.rationale: The institution is the registered party.

scenarios.stem: Which disclaimer element is mandatory on every screen?
options: Plain statement that content is educational, not advice, and that trading involves risk

scenarios.stem: An agent that fetches quotes, evaluates a rule, and sends an alert is:
options: An observer-only agent; the lowest-risk design

scenarios.stem: The agent reports "CHRW filled at 92.10." No fill exists in the broker. What happened?
options: Hallucination; the agent stated a result without a tool result
scenarios.rationale: Every fact must trace to a tool call.

scenarios.stem: Which check belongs outside the model, in code?
scenarios.rationale: Guardrails must not depend on the model obeying its prompt.

scenarios.stem: The system prompt says "never place market orders." Is that a guardrail?
options: No; it's an instruction the model could ignore, and must be enforced in the validation layer too
scenarios.rationale: Prompts are soft; code is hard.

scenarios.stem: The agent proposes a trade in JSON with symbol, action, size, reasoning, and invalidation. The invalidation field is empty. Correct response?
options: Reject; a proposal without an invalidation condition is incomplete
scenarios.rationale: Invalidation forces a falsifiable thesis.

scenarios.stem: Your scheduler fires the loop every minute during market hours. The rule uses daily bars. What is the problem?
options: Wasted calls and repeated alerts on the same daily signal
scenarios.rationale: Match cadence to bar timeframe.

scenarios.stem: The execution step crashed after submitting an order but before logging it. On restart, the agent resubmits. What was missing?
options: Idempotency via client order ID and a duplicate check

scenarios.stem: Which should the agent call before proposing any order?
scenarios.rationale: Dry run shows cost, fees, and buying-power impact.

scenarios.stem: The approval gate sends a Slack message. A subscriber's teenager taps "approve." What's the design flaw?
options: Approval must be authenticated, not just clickable

scenarios.stem: The agent's reasoning says "RSI is 28, strong buy." RSI from the tool result is 41. Diagnosis?
options: The model reasoned from stale or invented data; reject and log
scenarios.rationale: Compare reasoning against the actual tool output.

scenarios.stem: You backtest a rule and it returns 60% a year over five years after tuning eight parameters. What should you suspect?
scenarios.rationale: Many parameters, one dataset.

scenarios.stem: Best practice for backtesting a rule?
options: Tune on one period, test on a later unseen period
scenarios.rationale: Out-of-sample testing.

scenarios.stem: The kill switch halts the loop but leaves open limit orders resting. Complete?
options: No; kill must also cancel open orders

scenarios.stem: Audit log entries can be edited by the agent. Problem?
options: Logs must be append-only; a mutable log isn't an audit trail

scenarios.stem: Which is the correct order of steps in the loop?
options: Observe → reason → propose → approve → act → log

scenarios.stem: The agent is given the broker's full tool set including place_order, but the spec says observer-only. Fix?
options: Expose only the read tools; capability should match the spec
scenarios.rationale: Least privilege.

scenarios.stem: A rule file says: `flag when RSI < 35`. What's missing for it to be executable?
options: Symbol universe, bar timeframe, session, and RSI period

scenarios.stem: Two agents — proposer and compliance checker — disagree. Who wins?
options: Compliance checker; it exists to veto

scenarios.stem: The model returns prose instead of the JSON schema. Correct handling?
options: Reject, retry with schema enforcement, log the failure

scenarios.stem: The agent's weekly review shows three alerts fired correctly, one fired on a bad-data bar (a zero-volume print). Action?
options: Add a data-quality guard (minimum volume, sanity bounds)
scenarios.rationale: Fix the cause, not the symptom.

scenarios.stem: Rate limit hit mid-loop; quotes are missing for two symbols. The agent proposes trades on all five. Flaw?
options: Proposals on symbols with no fresh data must be blocked

scenarios.stem: Which belongs in the system prompt?
options: Role, allowed actions, forbidden actions, output schema
scenarios.rationale: Secrets never go in prompts; live data comes from tools.

scenarios.stem: A subscriber's agent has run 300 paper round trips with positive expectancy. What can you claim on the site?
options: Nothing performance-related; you can teach the method

scenarios.stem: The agent suggests adding a news-sentiment tool. What's the first guardrail question?
options: Can the source be logged and verified, and can the model be forced to cite it rather than paraphrase from memory?

scenarios.stem: Capstone: what is the minimum artifact set to prove a supervised round trip?
options: Rule file, audit log with trigger and approval, broker fill records, journal entry, post-mortem
